summary: This informational document describes OCRA, a challenge-response algorithm from OATH. It builds on HOTP and offers one-way and mutual authentication and electronic signature capabilities.

eli5.summary: A site asks a question and your token answers using a shared secret, proving you hold it without sending the secret.

questions: what is the difference between hotp and ocra
subtitle: Challenge-response authentication using HOTP with configurable input parameters

tldr.problem: The existing HOTP one-time password algorithm works with a counter, but many authentication scenarios need challenge-response mode where a server sends a random challenge and the client responds with a proof derived from that challenge. Different applications need different input combinations, output lengths, and signature capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: OCRA extends HOTP to accept various inputs—challenges, counters, PINs, session information, and timestamps—all specified in an OCRASuite string. The algorithm combines the selected inputs with a shared secret and applies HMAC with a selectable hash function (SHA-1, SHA-256, or SHA-512) followed by dynamic truncation to produce the response.
tldr.outcome: A standardized, flexible challenge-response algorithm that supports one-way authentication, mutual authentication between client and server, and short electronic signatures, all implementable in both hardware tokens and software applications.

today: OCRA was published as an Informational RFC in June 2011 and provides a standardized challenge-response algorithm that enables interoperability across multiple vendors' authentication products.

sections.title: Challenge-Response Authentication
sections.content:
OCRA (OATH Challenge-Response Algorithm) is a standardized challenge-response authentication mechanism developed by the Initiative for Open Authentication (OATH). Unlike HOTP, which uses an incrementing counter, OCRA is designed around a verifier sending a random challenge to the prover, who must respond with a proof of knowledge derived from that challenge and their secret key.

The motivation for OCRA comes from the observation that synchronous authentication systems like HOTP require the token and server to maintain a shared counter state. Challenge-response is asynchronous and does not require such synchronization, making it suitable for users and systems that cannot maintain shared state. The OATH initiative identified the need for a standardized algorithm to replace the many vendor-specific proprietary challenge-response schemes in the market.

OCRA supports not only one-way challenge-response (client proves identity to server) but also mutual authentication (server proves identity to client), and short electronic signatures where the data to be signed becomes the challenge. The algorithm is flexible enough to accommodate different token and application capabilities.
sections.eli5: Before OCRA, many companies made their own secret question-and-answer systems that did not work with other vendors' products. OCRA is a standard recipe anyone can use. It is good for tokens that do not keep track of how many times they have been used, and it lets both sides prove they are the real deal.

sections.title: How OCRA Works
sections.content:
OCRA is defined as OCRA = CryptoFunction(K, DataInput), where K is a shared secret key known to both parties and DataInput is a structure containing the inputs specified in the OCRASuite configuration string.

The DataInput structure is a concatenation of several optional fields: a counter (C), an optional challenge question (Q, always mandatory for the computation), a PIN/password hash (P), session information (S), and a timestamp (T). The challenge is always present and can be up to 128 bytes; if shorter, it is padded with zeros. The counter, if included, is an 8-byte value that can be used for synchronization. The PIN is a cryptographic hash of a PIN or password. Session information is UTF-8 encoded and can include session identifiers from the underlying connection. Timestamps represent time since epoch in the specified granularity (seconds, minutes, hours, or days).

The default CryptoFunction is HOTP-SHA1-6: HMAC-SHA1 applied to the DataInput, followed by dynamic truncation to produce a 6-digit decimal value. Other variants use SHA-256 or SHA-512 as the hash function and can produce 4 to 10 digit values, or even the full HMAC output without truncation.
sections.eli5: You take a secret, mix it with the question the server asked, add optional extras like a PIN or time, run it through a secure hash function, and chop off a few digits. Only someone with the secret can compute the same answer.

sections.title: Authentication and Signature Modes
sections.content:
One-Way Challenge-Response: The server sends a random challenge Q to the client. The client computes Response = OCRA(K, challenge) and sends it back. The server independently computes the same value and checks if they match. If they do, the client is authenticated. The inputs are typically counter (optional), challenge (mandatory), PIN hash (optional), session information (optional), and timestamp (optional).

Mutual Challenge-Response: Both parties challenge each other. The client first sends a client-challenge QC to the server. The server computes a server response using its key and sends back both its response and a server-challenge QS. The client verifies the server response by computing it independently using QC and QS. If valid, the client computes its own response using the reversed order of challenges (QS then QC) and optionally a PIN, then sends it to the server. The server verifies this client response. This provides two-way authentication.

Plain Signature: A signature mode where the data to be signed (or a hash of it) becomes the challenge. The client computes a signature by running the data (or challenge derived from it) through OCRA. The server verifies by computing the same value. This creates a symmetric key based short signature, useful for transaction signing in e-commerce.

Signature with Server Authentication: Combines signature mode with mutual authentication. The client sends a challenge first, the server responds with its own signature and the challenge to be signed, the client verifies the server signature, then signs the server's challenge.
sections.eli5: One-way is simple: you answer a question to prove you are you. Mutual is both of you asking each other questions. Signature mode is when you sign off on something, like approving a transaction. All modes use the same basic algorithm, just with different inputs in different orders.

sections.title: The OCRASuite Configuration String
sections.content:
An OCRASuite is a text string that completely specifies one OCRA mode. It has the format: <Algorithm>:<CryptoFunction>:<DataInput>

The Algorithm field specifies the version of OCRA (currently just OCRA-1). The CryptoFunction specifies the hash algorithm and output length, such as HOTP-SHA256-6 (SHA-256 with 6-digit truncation) or HOTP-SHA512-8 (SHA-512 with 8-digit truncation). The DataInput component specifies which inputs are used. For example, 'C' means include a counter, 'QN08' means numeric challenge up to 8 digits, 'PSHA1' means include a SHA-1 hash of a PIN, 'S512' means session information (512 bytes), and 'T1M' means timestamp in 1-minute granularity.

Examples: 'OCRA-1:HOTP-SHA256-6:QN08' is OCRA version 1 using SHA-256 truncated to 6 digits with a numeric challenge up to 8 digits and nothing else. 'OCRA-1:HOTP-SHA512-8:C-QN08-PSHA1-S512-T1M' includes counter, numeric challenge, PIN hash, 512 bytes of session data, and timestamp.

Client and server must agree on one OCRASuite for one-way modes and typically two OCRASuites (one for server computation, one for client computation) for mutual authentication or signature modes.
sections.eli5: The OCRASuite is a recipe card that says exactly what ingredients to use and how much of each. 'HOTP-SHA256-6:QN08' means use SHA-256 and 6 digits, with a numeric challenge up to 8 digits. The server and your token must use the same recipe.

sections.title: Security Properties and Deployment
sections.content:
OCRA's security depends on the strength of the underlying HOTP algorithm and the shared secret key. The best attack against HOTP is brute force. Keys SHOULD be at least as long as the HOTP output. Challenge values SHOULD be at least 20 bytes long and MUST be at least t bytes, where t is the output length in digits.

Critical implementation considerations: all communications SHOULD use secure channels (TLS or IPsec). Keys MUST be generated randomly or using a cryptographically strong pseudo-random generator. Keys on the client side SHOULD be in tamper-resistant devices (hardware tokens) or secure software implementations. On the server side, keys MUST be stored encrypted and decrypted only when needed, to limit their exposure in memory.

In signature modes where counter and timestamp are not used, there is a risk of replay attacks, and implementations should mitigate this through application-specific mechanisms. When using mutual authentication or signature with server authentication, implementations MAY use a dual-key approach where different keys are used for server and client computations, further isolating the compromise of one key.

The inclusion of session information (S) is RECOMMENDED to bind the OCRA response to a specific session, which can mitigate man-in-the-middle attacks, though it requires the prover and verifier to both have access to the session identifier.
sections.eli5: Keep your secrets random and long. Use trusted networks. On your phone or token, lock up the secret. On the server, only unlock the secret when you need it. When signing things, always include something time-dependent or session-specific so old signatures cannot be reused.

sections.title: Status and Adoption
sections.content:
OCRA was published as an Informational RFC in June 2011. As an OATH standard, it provides a common specification that enables multiple vendors to produce interoperable authentication tokens and validation servers, reducing lock-in to proprietary solutions.

The algorithm is suitable for implementation in both hardware tokens (with built-in buttons and PIN pads for entering challenges) and software applications (on computers and mobile devices). The configurability of OCRASuite allows different deployments to choose the security level and feature set appropriate to their risk profile.

OCRA complements HOTP in scenarios where synchronization is problematic or where the flexibility of challenge-response is preferred. Organizations seeking to deploy strong authentication can use HOTP for time-based tokens and OCRA for challenge-response devices, both backed by the same OATH framework.
sections.eli5: OCRA is a published standard that anyone can use. Hardware token makers and software companies can build products that all use OCRA and work with each other's servers. This gives organizations choices instead of being locked into one vendor's system.
